claims.text: As a traditional sushi restaurant, dishes are served with standard Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat; this is the default and there is no documented gluten-free or wheat-free soy sauce option.
The kitchen centers on seafood from Omicho Market and dashi-based soup, so cross-contact with fish is unavoidable; no separate vegan preparation is documented.
The kitchen prepares tempura and other fried seafood/vegetable dishes, so shared frying oil and wheat batter make gluten cross-contact likely.
As a traditional Kanazawa izakaya, dishes rely on regular (wheat-containing) soy sauce, miso, and seasonings; no wheat-free soy sauce is documented.
The menu is seafood- and meat-forward (nodoguro, sashimi, Noto-beef stew); vegetable dishes are typically finished with fish dashi, so no reliably vegan preparation is documented.
The kitchen centers on buckwheat soba (typically cut with wheat) plus tempura and soy/dashi seasonings, so wheat is pervasive across the fixed courses.
Courses are built on seafood, duck, and dashi; no plant-based course is documented and the menu is fixed by the kitchen.
Headline sweets are naturally plant-based and bean/agar-based: black beans set in agar with a syrup made from the beans' own cooking liquid, and bean shiruko made from heirloom beans.
Seasonal bean soup is served with simply prepared vegetables and pickles, indicating a strongly plant-forward kitchen.
Wheat ramen noodles are boiled in the same kitchen; no gluten-free preparation documented.
Miso-based broths at ramen shops typically contain wheat-derived miso and soy ingredients; no allergen-free claims documented.
Broth is pork-bone based with pork toppings; no separate vegan preparation documented.

name: Meringue (お好み焼き 鉄板バル メレンゲ)

claims.text: It is a 鉄板バル cooking やきそば (wheat noodles) and a 「金澤野菜のサラダそば」 (soba, normally wheat-blended) on the same teppan as the flourless okonomiyaki — shared-griddle cross-contact is likely. All-counter room; no clean-surface protocol published.

The finishing okonomiyaki ソース/オリジナルソース ingredients are undocumented. Standard okonomiyaki sauce contains wheat and soy sauce; no tamari/GF sauce is confirmed, so sauced okonomiyaki cannot be assumed gluten-free.
Egg-white-meringue batter plus pork/seafood — not vegan.

Shop markets the okonomiyaki as グルテンフリー based on the flourless batter, but no allergen/sauce/cross-contact statement is published; Tabelog flags the venue as relocated and the official domain was unreachable at last check.
Genuinely flourless okonomiyaki — batter uses egg-white meringue instead of wheat flour (小麦粉不使用), a rare celiac-friendly base.

name: もりもり寿し 近江町店 (Morimori Sushi Omicho-ten)

claims.text: Conveyor-belt sushi using standard wheat-based soy sauce and vinegared rice; no gluten-free handling is documented, so cross-contact with wheat is likely.
Standard Japanese soy sauce (contains wheat) is used at the counter; no wheat-free tamari is mentioned.
Menu is built around raw fish, shellfish and seafood; no vegan items are documented and shared surfaces handle seafood.
Multilingual menus (English, Simplified and Traditional Chinese, Korean) make it easier to identify and avoid specific ingredients.

name: むすび 近江町市場店 (Musubi Omicho Ichiba-ten)

claims.text: Wheat-breaded croquettes are sold and fried at the same small stall as the rice products, with no documented separation.
Soy sauce-based onigiri fillings are common at such shops and standard Japanese soy sauce contains wheat; no wheat-free soy sauce is documented.
Fish, meat, and mayonnaise fillings are prepared alongside any plain rice balls at the same counter; no separation is documented.
Naturally simple options like plain salt, umeboshi (pickled plum), or kombu onigiri may suit some diners, though fillings should be confirmed in person.
